name: Antisemitism
info: Antisemitism is hostility to, prejudice towards, or discrimination against Jews; it grew out of Christian anti-Judaism, took its name and racial form in 19th-century Europe, and ran from discrimination and pogroms to the Nazi genocide.

facts.thinkers: Wilhelm Marr, who coined Antisemitismus and founded the Antisemiten-Liga in 1879; Moritz Steinschneider, who used the word antisemitische in 1860 against Ernest Renan; Joseph Arthur de Gobineau, a racial theorist; Heinrich von Treitschke, who coined “the Jews are our misfortune”; Richard Wagner; Louis de Bonald; Édouard Drumont; Adolf Stoecker; Leon Pinsker, who called it Judeophobia
facts.texts: Wagner’s Das Judenthum in der Musik (1850); Gobineau’s Essay on the Inequality of the Human Race (1853–1855); Marr’s Der Sieg des Judenthums über das Germanenthum (1879); Luther’s On the Jews and their Lies (1543); Bonald’s Sur les juifs (1806); Gougenot des Mousseaux’s Le Juif, le judaïsme et la judaïsation des peuples chrétiens (1869); The Protocols of the Elders of Zion, a forgery published in Russia in 1903
facts.ideas: that Jews form a distinct and inferior race; that Jews are an alien collective within host nations; that Jews control finance and seek world power through a secret conspiracy; that Jews corrupt a nation’s culture; that Jews are collectively guilty of killing Christ; that Jews are responsible for political and economic crises
facts.today: antisemitism in far-right politics and violence, in Holocaust denial, in conspiracy theories in Europe and the Arab world, and a rise in anti-Jewish hate crimes after October 2023; scholars dispute the concept of a “new antisemitism” and the definitions in use

t: The term Antisemitismus was first printed in Germany in 1879 as a scientific-sounding word for Judenhass, but anti-Jewish sentiment is traced to the 3rd century BCE, and scholars debate whether earlier hostility belongs under the same name.

Religious antisemitism, rooted in the conflict between Judaism and Christianity, was joined in the 19th century by racial antisemitism, which held that Jews were a distinct and inferior race and that baptism did not change this.
Racial antisemitism culminated in Nazi Germany, where eleven million Jews were targeted for extermination and some six million were killed in the Holocaust.
dyk: The word antisemitic was first used in 1860 by Moritz Steinschneider to characterise Ernest Renan’s ideas about “Semitic races”; Wilhelm Marr’s league of 1879 made it the name of a political cause.
ev: Antiochus IV Epiphanes erects an altar to Zeus in the Temple and bans circumcision, Shabbat and Torah study, sparking the Maccabean Revolt
Hundreds or thousands of Jews are killed during the First Crusade, the first major outbreak of anti-Jewish violence in Christian Europe outside Spain
Jews are blamed for the Black Death; 900 are burned alive in Strasbourg and Pope Clement VI issues two bulls to protect them
Martin Luther writes On the Jews and their Lies, recommending a pogrom against them
Wilhelm Marr publishes The Victory of the Jewish Spirit over the Germanic Spirit and founds the Antisemiten-Liga
The Nuremberg Laws forbid marriages between Aryans and Jews and strip German Jews of full citizenship
The Kristallnacht pogrom of 9–10 November kills at least 91 Jews and burns or damages about 1,400 synagogues
The mass murder by the Einsatzgruppen that began in 1941 culminates in the systematic genocide of the Holocaust

sections.origins:
Many authors see the roots of modern antisemitism in both pagan antiquity and early Christianity. The first clear examples of anti-Jewish sentiment can be traced to the 3rd century BCE in Alexandria, where the Egyptian priest and historian Manetho wrote scathingly of the Jews. Antiochus IV Epiphanes issued one of the earliest anti-Jewish edicts, in about 170–167 BCE, which sparked the revolt of the Maccabees. Edward Flannery describes ancient antisemitism as essentially cultural, a national xenophobia played out in political settings, while Bohak has argued that early animosity is not antisemitic unless it was held against the Jews alone, since many Greeks showed animosity toward any group they regarded as barbarians.

As Christianity became the dominant religion, increasingly restrictive legislation and rhetoric was directed against Jews. Religious antisemitism, also called anti-Judaism, is antipathy towards Jews because of their perceived religious beliefs, typically with doctrines of supersession that expect Jews to turn away from Judaism.

The word itself is newer. Moritz Steinschneider used antisemitische Vorurteile in 1860 against Ernest Renan, and in 1879 the German journalist Wilhelm Marr used Antisemitismus in a popular pamphlet, accusing the Jews of a worldwide conspiracy against non-Jews. In the same year he founded the Antisemiten-Liga, the first German organisation committed specifically to combating the alleged threat the Jews posed to German culture and advocating their forced removal. The word entered English from German in 1881.
sections.ideas:
Antisemitism is not a single doctrine, and writers have offered several taxonomies of it. Bernard Lazare, writing in the 1890s, named Christian, economic and ethnologic antisemitism; William Brustein names religious, racial, economic and political forms; Louis Harap adds social, ideological and cultural ones. Dietz Bering writes that, to antisemites, Jews are totally bad by nature and their traits incorrigible, so that Jews are to be seen as a collective, remain alien in the societies around them, and secretly bring disaster on their host societies or on the world.

Racial antisemitism held that Jews are a distinct and inferior race compared to their host nations. It gained mainstream acceptance in the late 19th and early 20th centuries as part of the eugenics movement, drew on the racial theory of Joseph Arthur de Gobineau and on Social Darwinism, and claimed the superiority of northern European “Aryans” over “Semitic” Jews. Its holders saw Jews as beyond redemption even if they converted, whereas religious antisemitism in theory ended with conversion. The race theories behind it were pseudoscientific.

Economic antisemitism rests on the claim that Jews perform harmful economic activities, above all that they control the world’s finances; the forged Protocols of the Elders of Zion promoted this, and Henry Ford repeated it. Political antisemitism, in William Brustein’s definition, is hostility based on the belief that Jews seek national or world power. Cultural antisemitism, in Louis Harap’s, charges the Jews with corrupting a culture and supplanting it.
sections.spread:
In the Middle Ages the Visigothic kingdom in Hispania issued anti-Jewish edicts from the late 6th century. Under Islamic rule Jews were classed as dhimmis and could practise more freely than in Christian Europe, but pogroms took place in Córdoba in 1011 and Granada in 1066, and the Almohads, who had taken control of the Maghrib and Andalusia by 1147, treated dhimmis harshly. In Christian Europe Jews were persecuted with blood libels, expulsions, forced conversions and massacres, with a first peak during the Crusades. Jews were banished from England in 1290, 100,000 were expelled from France in 1394, and in 1348 they were made scapegoats for the Black Death. Martin Luther’s pamphlet of 1543 is called by Paul Johnson the first work of modern antisemitism.

In the Russian Empire Catherine II confined Jews to the Pale of Settlement in 1772, and the May Laws of 1882 followed the assassination of Alexander II. The Dreyfus Affair in France began in 1894, and Karl Lueger in Vienna and Adolf Stoecker in Germany used antisemitism in politics. In the United States antisemitism reached its peak in the interwar period; Henry Ford’s The Dearborn Independent ran from 1919 to 1927. Since the early 20th century incidents rose sharply across the Arab world, largely through Arab conspiracy theories influenced by European ones.
sections.power:
After Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party came to power in 1933, the German government instituted repressive legislation that denied Jews basic civil rights. The Nuremberg Laws of September 1935 prohibited marriages and sexual relations between “Aryans” and Jews and stripped all German Jews of full citizenship. In the state-sponsored pogrom of 9–10 November 1938, Kristallnacht, at least 91 Jews were killed, thousands were arrested, over 7,500 Jewish businesses were destroyed and about 1,400 synagogues were burned or damaged. After war began in 1939, antisemitic legislation and propaganda were extended to German-occupied Europe, often adapting local traditions, as in Vichy France and occupied Poland. Jews were forced into ghettos in Warsaw, Kraków, Lvov, Lublin and Radom.

After the attack on the Soviet Union in 1941, mass murder by the Einsatzgruppen culminated from 1942 to 1945 in systematic genocide, the Holocaust. Eleven million Jews were targeted for extermination by the Nazis, and some six million were eventually killed.

Other states also practised it. Close to 50,000 Jews were killed in pogroms during the Russian Civil War. In the Soviet Union a campaign against “rootless cosmopolitans”, a euphemism for Jews, began after 1948, and Yiddish-language poets, writers and artists were killed or arrested; the fabricated Doctors’ Plot of 1952 led to the arrest and execution of Jewish professionals, and the Slánský show trial of the same year alleged an international Zionist conspiracy. After the Kielce pogrom, Polish Jewish survivors fled postwar Poland.
sections.critiques:
Scholars dispute both the definition and the history. The eternalist view sees antisemitism as separate from other prejudice, a transhistorical force culminating in the Holocaust; Hannah Arendt criticised it for answering “Why the Jews of all people?” with “Eternal hostility”. The contextual view treats it as a type of racism tied to its historical setting, and David Engel argues that the term implies links between anti-Jewish prejudices of different contexts without evidence of them.

Its causes are explained in competing ways. Theodor Adorno wrote that “Anti-Semitism is the rumour about the Jews”. Bernard Lazare’s 1894 book argued that Jewish separateness helped cause hostility, a belief he later abandoned. Julie Mell’s scholarship finds Jews were not overrepresented in medieval moneylending and that the greed stereotype projected Christian taboos on the minority. David Nirenberg argues antisemitism is embedded in Western thought and adapts to each period. Some scholars read Karl Marx’s “On the Jewish Question” as antisemitic; Francis Wheen and David McLellan argue it was written as a defence of the Jews against Bruno Bauer.

The 2016 IHRA working definition is among the most controversial documents on the subject, with critics arguing it has been used to censor criticism of Israel; the Nexus Document and the Jerusalem Declaration followed in 2021. Proponents of a “new antisemitism” argue that anti-Zionism can serve as a vehicle for attacks on Jews, while critics say the concept silences debate on Israel.
sections.legacy:
After 1945, and especially once the full extent of the Nazi genocide was known, the word antisemitism took on a pejorative sense; Yehuda Bauer wrote in 1984 that nobody now says “I am anti-Semitic”, whereas before the Second World War it was not uncommon for a person or a party to call itself antisemitic. Style guides, the Associated Press from 2021 among them, now favour the unhyphenated spelling, in part because, as Emil Fackenheim argued in 2003, it avoids implying an entity called “Semitism”.

Antisemitism persists in contemporary far-right politics and has been a factor for perpetrators of violence such as the Pittsburgh and Poway synagogue shooters, and Holocaust denial and conspiracy theories are counted among its forms. Attacks on Jewish memorials, synagogues and cemeteries in Europe rose after the economic crisis of 2008, and a significant increase in anti-Jewish hate crimes worldwide after the Hamas-led attack on Israel of 7 October 2023. A July 2026 report by the J7 task force found more than 20 people killed in antisemitic incidents in seven countries in 2025.

Education is a stated remedy, though Dara Horn argues that teaching it through the Holocaust is unhelpful and proposes curiosity about Jewish life instead. The study of antisemitism remains politically contested because of differing interpretations of the Holocaust and of the Israeli–Palestinian conflict.

summary: Antisemitism is hostility to or discrimination against Jews, rooted in ancient prejudice and Christian anti-Judaism and named in Germany in 1879. Its racial form culminated in the Nazi genocide of some six million Jews, and scholars still dispute how to define it.
references: Steven Beller, Antisemitism: A Very Short Introduction (Oxford University Press, 2007)
Walter Laqueur, The Changing Face of Antisemitism: From Ancient Times to the Present Day (Oxford University Press, 2006)
Bernard Lewis, Semites and Anti-Semites: an Inquiry into Conflict and Prejudice (W. W. Norton & Company, 1999)
Marvin Perry, Antisemitism: Myth and Hate from Antiquity to the Present (Palgrave Macmillan, 2002)
Raul Hilberg, The Destruction of the European Jews (Holmes & Meier, 1985)
notes: Start 1879, circa true: the article dates the word Antisemitismus and Marr's league to 1879 (widely printed 1881; Steinschneider's earlier use 1860), but traces anti-Jewish sentiment to the 3rd century BCE and says the term is also applied to earlier incidents. Whether earlier hostility is 'antisemitism' is disputed (Bohak, Engel); both positions are in the text.
The article names no references in its saved text (the reference and further reading sections are empty), so references is [].

Article inconsistency: it gives the Almohads as controlling territories 'by 1147' and Marr's league 'apparently' named after the Anti-Chancellor League; I used only the first. The Antiochus date appears as 'about 170–167 BCE' and '167 BCE'; I used both as stated.

Figures kept as the article gives them: Kristallnacht 'at least 91' killed; 11 million targeted and 'some six million' killed; 'close to 50,000' in the Russian Civil War pogroms. The Khmelnytsky massacres (100,000 to 200,000 decrease, mixed causes) and the Uman massacre were left out as the figures mix causes.
Event 1942: the article says 'from 1942 to 1945' for systematic genocide; the Einsatzgruppen campaign began after 1941.

Left out: Voltaire, Lindbergh and Ford detail, Walt Whitman, the Grimms, the Arab antisemitism polls and clerics' epithets, Black Hebrew Israelite section, Pinsker's quotation, Penslar/Foxman lists, the Netanyahu/Husseini passage, Trump-era remarks, the 2024 House vote, and the unreliable passage on 19th-century Muslim lands (stone-throwing quotation), as contested or needing more context than space allows. The article contains typos ('emiration', 'cetury').

Hard point: ideas are given as claims of their holders; the article itself calls the racial theories pseudoscientific and the Protocols a forgery. No verdict is given on the IHRA or new-antisemitism debates.
